title: Possibly sacrilegious word of advice - if you’re seeing The Boy and the Heron in an English-speaking nation, choose the dub.

commenti.body:
The first two Ghibli movies I saw back in the ‘90s were *Kiki’s Delivery Service* and *Princess Mononoke.* I didn’t like either of them. When *Spirited Away* came to theaters I went to see it and was absolutely floored by how great it was. 

Why did I love that one but not the others? The difference was that *Spirited Away* was distributed in Japanese with English Subtitles while the previous two were only available with the English dub. I went back and watched *Kiki* and *Mononoke* on Blu-Ray when they were available and loved both movies. 

What I learned was that experiencing an animated movie in its original language is just as important as it is for live action.

Exactly, I agree with everything you said and it’s why I assumed the dub would be lesser - this one is different. 

It’s not at all the same thing as live-action imo because in that you’re dealing with flesh-and-blood actors whose voices and words are being replaced by someone entirely different. There’s always going to be a fundamental disconnect, something uncanny and false, in a live action dub. 

Animation in its original language is already a voice actor giving life to a man made creation. It’s not substitution so much as recasting, there’s no inherent falsehood to it. It can feel that way when the dub is papered on as a method of basic translation, as it is with much anime including classic Ghibli. 

Again - this one is different. The voice work is easily the best I’ve heard in an animated film in a while. All of it feels true to the film. I implied this a little above, but I picked up on nuances in characterization and narrative that I totally missed when I saw it in Japanese. It also really helps to be able to devote your eyes entirely to the imagery.

This movie was incredible. It doesn’t even suffer from the problem that a lot of animated features do these days, where the voice actors are so famous and so recognizable that you’re keenly aware that you’re hearing “famous actor XYZ”. I made a point to avoid cast spoilers, and I was shocked once it got to the credits. Absolutely nobody phones it in on the dub, they’re all unrecognizable.

It blows my mind that Christian was Howl and wanted any role in a Miyazaki film after being blown away when he saw spirited away, and fucking Werner Herzog played the very Jewish man in The Wind Rises.

I think something important to note alongside any argument over whether the dub or sub version is “better” is that the Japanese and English performance styles are very, very different and create quite different experiences. In a situation like this where you are getting high quality either way, it’s largely just down to which style you prefer.

I personally have always held modern Ghibli English dubs to a very high standard for dubbing foreign films. There’s just about no celebrity-name casting, but rather VAs are for the most part well cast, worth their higher pay grades per the dramatic control they can bring, and for the most part, really want to be there, Casting paints a really interesting weave of associations, like how Miyazaki mentee, animator on Nausica and Anime pioneer Neon Genesis Evangelion creator Hideaki Anno voices the main character in The Wind Rises. It blows my mind that Christian Bale was Howl and wanted any role in a Miyazaki film after being blown away when he saw spirited away, and that it was fucking Werner Herzog who played the very Jewish man with the large nose in The Wind Rises.
